(1) inhibition of FAO in the heart does not protect from heart failure, (2) inhibition of FA transport and FA oxidation in the heart is detrimental in ischaemic heart failure and (3) inhibition of FA oxidation is protective in non-ischaemic models of heart failure.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel strategies for the treatment of heart failure.
a better understanding of the complex interplay between the metabolic pathways and their role in the development of heart failure and how these might be exploited for therapeutic intervention.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
inhibition of FAO is not beneficial in all forms of heart failure.
the shift in substrate preference in heart failure is a double-edged sword, which might not only be beneficial for the failing hearts, but also harmful.
the shift in cardiac energy metabolism towards increased glucose utilization is detrimental to cardiac function and that the heart should rely on FA metabolism for energy supply in heart failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the beneficial effects of FAO inhibition in heart failure are not due to an increased reliance on glucose utilization but to the inhibition of the pro-apoptotic effects of fatty acyl CoA esters.
FA metabolism is not simply good or bad, but that its effects are dependent on the type of heart failure, the severity of disease and the stage of heart failure.
inhibition of FAO in the early phase of heart failure is detrimental for the heart, while in the late phase it may be beneficial for heart function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the consequences of modulations in cardiac FA metabolism are context-dependent.
inhibition of FAO is beneficial in the early stages of ischaemic injury but detrimental in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies.
the beneficial effects of FAO are not only limited to the ischaemic myocardium but also extend into the non-ischaemic myocardium.
